text.text: A speech sound is produced by a source and shaped by a filter. The source is either the quasi-periodic puffs of air let through by the vibrating vocal folds (voicing), turbulent noise at a narrowing (whisper, aspiration, frication), or both. The filter is the air in the vocal tract from the larynx to the lips (and the nose, when the velum is lowered), whose resonances, the formants, depend on its shape; the radiated sound is the flow at the lips, differentiated by radiation into the open air. If the tract is treated as a linear, time-invariant system over stretches of a few tens of milliseconds, the output spectrum is the product P(f)=S(f) T(f) R(f),LP(f)=LS(f)+LT(f)+LR(f)(decibels),\begin{aligned}P(f)&=S(f)\,T(f)\,R(f),\\L_P(f)&=L_S(f)+L_T(f)\\&\quad+L_R(f)\quad\text{(decibels),}\end{aligned}P(f)LP​(f)​=S(f)T(f)R(f),=LS​(f)+LT​(f)+LR​(f)(decibels),​ of the source spectrum SSS (lines at the harmonics kf0k f_0kf0​ of the voice, falling about 12 dB per octave, or a flat noise continuum), the tract's transfer function TTT (peaks at the formants) and the radiation characteristic RRR (rising about 6 dB per octave). The larynx and the articulators work independently: the vocal folds set pitch and voice quality, the tongue, lips and jaw set the formants.Holds when Holds when the vocal tract can be treated as a linear, time-invariant filter (sound pressures far below the steady airflow, shapes changing slowly compared with the period) and the source is unaffected by the tract. It is only approximate when the two interact: high voices whose f0f_0f0​ approaches F1, rapid articulatory movements, and nasal coupling, which adds antiresonances.

Because the tract filters linearly, convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, so each harmonic of the source is simply scaled by the gain of the filter at its frequency. A periodic source has a line spectrum (its Fourier series), so voiced speech is a picket fence of harmonics whose heights trace the filter's resonance curve, while a noise source gives a continuous spectrum with the same peaks. The idea goes back to Johannes Müller's experiments with excised larynges in the 1830s; Chiba and Kajiyama (1941) computed the tract's resonances, and Gunnar Fant's Acoustic Theory of Speech Production (1960) made source × filter the standard model; the formant model of timbre is music-4.10.The harmonic-by-harmonic step uses the LTI eigenfunction calculation (sig 3.9): for an absolutely integrable impulse response hhh, inserting eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt in the convolution integral gives eiωt∫h(τ)e−iωτ dτe^{i\omega t}\int h(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\taueiωt∫h(τ)e−iωτdτ. Thus each harmonic retains its frequency and acquires the transfer factor at that frequency. Apply this integral calculation to the tract response when that hypothesis holds over a fixed-shape window. Ideal radiation differentiation is a separate operation: ddteiωt=iωeiωt\frac{d}{dt}e^{i\omega t}=i\omega e^{i\omega t}dtd​eiωt=iωeiωt, rather than an absolutely integrable impulse response. Neither step asserts exact linearity or independence of the source and tract in actual speech.

Drag the F1, F2, F3 handles on the middle panel to reshape the filter, or pick a preset. The left panel is the source, the right one the output: every harmonic of the output is the source harmonic raised by the filter's gain at that frequency, and the readout checks this against the spectrum of the waveform actually synthesized (time domain, then FFT). Change the pitch: the harmonics slide, the envelope stays. Switch the source to whisper: the harmonics vanish but the formant peaks (and the vowel) remain. Source alone plays the buzz before the tract shapes it. (The lip radiation is folded into the source here.)

text.text: The same vowel spoken by different people has very different formant frequencies: children's formants are up to 40–50 % higher than men's because their vocal tracts are shorter, and women's lie in between. In raw hertz the vowel categories of a population therefore overlap heavily (a child's [ʊ] can have the formants of a man's [ʌ]), yet listeners identify vowels across speakers almost effortlessly. They do so by normalising: judging each vowel relative to the speaker's own vowel space. Computational normalisations that rescale each speaker's formants, for example the log-mean method (Nearey), which subtracts the speaker's mean log formant, or Lobanov's z-scores, which standardise each formant by the speaker's mean and standard deviation, make the categories of different speakers line up and greatly reduce the overlap.

To a first approximation a shorter vocal tract multiplies all formants by the same factor (resonances scale as 1/L1/L1/L, ling-1.8), so on a logarithmic scale a speaker's whole vowel space is shifted rigidly. Subtracting the speaker's mean log formant undoes that shift (Nearey 1978); Lobanov's (1971) z-scores also undo differences in the spread of the space. Listeners appear to use similar information, both from the other vowels they have heard from the speaker (extrinsic normalisation) and from cues within the vowel such as f0f_0f0​ and F3 (intrinsic). The data here are simulated: each speaker's vowels are drawn around Peterson and Barney's group means (ling-1.9), scaled by a random vocal-tract factor and given random token-to-token variation.The logarithm law (pma 8.6) supplies the cancellation in log-mean normalisation. If all positive formant measurements FiF_iFi​ are multiplied by one speaker factor a>0a>0a>0, then log⁡(aFi)=log⁡a+log⁡Fi\log(aF_i)=\log a+\log F_ilog(aFi​)=loga+logFi​ and their mean log shifts by the same log⁡a\log aloga. Subtraction therefore leaves every centred log coordinate unchanged. This exact invariance belongs to the common-multiplier model; unequal formant scaling, different vowel sampling and biological differences are not removed by that identity.

Each symbol is one vowel token of one simulated speaker (8 men, 8 women, 8 children); ellipses enclose about 80 % of each vowel category. Switch the normalisation: in raw hertz the ellipses sprawl and overlap, after log-mean or Lobanov normalisation they shrink and separate. The readout scores each method by classifying every token with the category centres learned from the other speakers (nearest centre, leave one speaker out). Highlight a group to see its own vowel space; New speakers draws another population.

When listeners hear a continuum of synthetic syllables whose voice onset time increases in equal steps from [ba] to [pa], they do not hear a gradual change: identification stays near 100 % /b/ up to a boundary (about 25 ms VOT for English labials), then switches to /p/ within one or two steps. Discrimination follows the labels: two stimuli 20 ms apart are told apart well when they straddle the boundary and barely above chance when both fall in the same category, although the acoustic difference is the same. Perception of this kind, where discrimination is predicted by identification, is called categorical perception. It is strong for stop consonants and much weaker for vowels, and it is shaped by the listener's language: the boundary sits where the language's categories need it.

If listeners could only compare category labels, the probability of answering an ABX trial correctly (is X the same as A or as B?) would be 12+12(pA−pB)2\tfrac12+\tfrac12(p_A-p_B)^221​+21​(pA​−pB​)2, where pA,pBp_A, p_BpA​,pB​ are the probabilities of labelling A and B as /p/: discrimination is then at chance within a category and peaks at the boundary. Liberman, Harris, Hoffman and Griffith (1957) found that real discrimination of stop continua nearly matches this prediction. Later work showed it is not purely categorical (listeners do hear some within-category differences, given sensitive tasks), and that chinchillas and infants show similar VOT boundaries, so part of the effect is auditory; but the boundary's location is tuned by experience with a language (ling-1.5).The label-only ABX prediction assumes fresh independent Bernoulli labels for A, B and X, with probabilities pA,pBp_A,p_BpA​,pB​ of the /p/ label, and balanced choices of whether X repeats A or B. When A and B receive the same label, the decision is a random tie; otherwise it matches X's label. Factoring products of these bounded independent label indicators (prob 2.1.13) and summing the eight label outcomes gives 12+12(pA−pB)2\tfrac12+\tfrac12(p_A-p_B)^221​+21​(pA​−pB​)2. Independence and the tie rule are premises of this prediction, not measured properties of a listener, so the formula is not a universal discrimination law.

The dispersion theory of vowel systems (Liljencrants and Lindblom, 1972) proposes that languages choose vowels that are as far apart as possible in auditory space, so that they are easy to tell apart. Model each vowel as a point in the space of possible vowels, measured by its first two formants on an auditory (Bark) scale, and choose nnn points that minimise the total "energy" E=∑i<j1/dij2E=\sum_{i<j}1/d_{ij}^2E=∑i<j​1/dij2​, where dijd_{ij}dij​ is the auditory distance between vowels iii and jjj. The optima for small nnn reproduce the patterns of the commonest inventories of the world's languages: three vowels go to the corners [i a u], and five spread into two front, one low and two back vowels, the pattern of the most frequent system [i e a o u]. For larger nnn the simple model predicts too many high vowels (central [ɨ]-like vowels) compared with real languages, which add mid vowels instead, such as the common seven-vowel [i e ɛ a ɔ o u].Holds when A model of which vowel qualities languages prefer, valid statistically across languages rather than for any one language; it ignores length, nasality, rounding as a separate dimension, and the role of focal (stable) vowels, and it overpredicts high vowels for systems of more than about seven.

The repulsive energy pushes points apart like charges confined to a region, so they first occupy the corners of the vowel space and then spread along its edge: the edge is longest along the front–back dimension at the top (high vowels have the widest F2 range), so the optimum fills the periphery and avoids the centre. The space itself is the triangle-like region reachable by the vocal tract, here the hull of the measured cardinal vowels (ling-1.9). Weighting F2 less (because higher formants are perceived less sharply) shrinks the top edge and improves the predictions for larger systems, an observation that led to refinements such as Schwartz and colleagues' dispersion–focalisation theory (1997).The ideal energy minimisation has an existence argument distinct from finding it numerically. For n≥2n\ge2n≥2 points in a compact auditory region containing nnn distinct feasible points, choose one collision-free configuration with finite energy E0E_0E0​. In its energy sublevel, every pair has distance at least E0−1/2E_0^{-1/2}E0−1/2​, so that sublevel is compact and avoids collisions. The energy is continuous there; the extreme-value theorem (pma 4.16) gives a minimum, also global since every lower-energy configuration lies in this sublevel. This proves existence in the declared model, not that a numerical search certifies the global minimum or that real languages optimise this objective.

The shaded region is the space of possible vowels (outline of the cardinal vowels, on Bark scales: F2 leftward, F1 downward). Choose the number of vowels and watch them repel each other to the configuration of least energy; each settles next to the nearest cardinal vowel symbol, named in the readout. Drag any vowel to disturb the system and see the others rearrange; Shake starts again from new random positions (the energy has local minima, so the best of ten starts is animated). Raise the F2 weight to 1 to see the model add extra high vowels, its best-known failure; lower it and mid vowels appear instead.

text.text: Phonemes are not atoms but bundles of binary distinctive features such as [±voice][\pm\text{voice}][±voice], [±nasal][\pm\text{nasal}][±nasal] and [±continuant][\pm\text{continuant}][±continuant]: each feature names one articulatory or acoustic property, and a segment is a column of +++ and −-− values (or 000, "not applicable"). A small number of features (a few dozen at most) suffices to tell apart the phonemes of any language, and phonological patterns are stated over features rather than over lists of sounds.

Each feature carves the inventory into two halves, so nnn binary features can distinguish up to 2n2^n2n segments; real inventories are far sparser than that because features are correlated (every nasal is voiced and sonorant). The reason to prefer features to symbols is that sounds sharing a feature behave alike in rules (2.4, 2.5): the set of sounds that trigger a rule is then a conjunction of feature values, a simple object, rather than an arbitrary list. The feature set used here is a simplified teaching system of 17 features: stridency, laterality and tenseness are handled coarsely, and [bk] is left unspecified (0) for schwa.The binary capacity count uses the product rule (comb 1.1): for nnn freely specifiable features with two values each, choosing one value at each coordinate gives exactly 2n2^n2n distinct bundles. An actual inventory occupies only some bundles because its features need not vary independently. The widget's value 000 means unspecified or inapplicable; it is not silently counted as one of the two signs in that binary bound.

Left: set each feature to +++, −-− or any (click a box). Right: the symbols that match every condition light up. Click a symbol on the chart to load its full feature column, then relax a feature to see which sounds join it; the presets set up classes you will meet in 2.4. Notice how few features it takes to isolate a single sound.

A set of segments is a natural class if some bundle of feature values picks out exactly its members and nothing else. Phonological rules overwhelmingly apply to, or are triggered by, natural classes, and the smaller the bundle needed, the more natural (and more frequent) the class. A set like {p,s,η,a}\{p, s, \eta, \mathrm{a}\}{p,s,η,a} that no bundle singles out is unnatural: any bundle covering all of its members also covers extra segments.

The segments matching a feature value form a set; a bundle selects the intersection of such sets. So natural classes are exactly the intersections of feature-value sets (2.3), a tiny family compared with all 2392^{39}239 subsets of the 39 symbols on the chart. To test a given set, intersect the feature values it shares: that intersection is the most specific bundle containing the whole set, and the set is natural exactly when this bundle selects nothing else. The tool then searches for the shortest bundle with the same extension.Make one predicate for each specified feature value, true of a segment exactly when that segment carries that value. Conjunction has the truth-table semantics of logic 2.3, so a bundle holds exactly when every selected predicate holds; its extension is therefore the intersection of their extensions. A 000 entry is not automatically the negation of a positive feature value. This is a finite interpretation on the displayed inventory, and it licenses the intersection test without treating arbitrary subsets as single natural classes.

Click symbols to build a set (gold). The readout finds the smallest feature bundle that defines it, or shows the smallest natural class that contains it — the extra members it drags in are marked red. Try the preset plural -s triggers (p t k f θ): it is natural, defined by the three values [+cons −voi −strid], which is why one rule suffices in 2.5. Then add /s/ or /ɑ/ and watch it stop being natural.

When a grammar has several rules, the order in which they apply can change the output. Rule XXX feeds rule YYY when applying XXX first creates new sites where YYY can apply, and bleeds it when applying XXX first destroys sites where YYY would apply. If the attested forms need XXX before YYY in the first case or YYY before XXX in the second, the order is extrinsic and must be part of the grammar. The reverse orders, in which a rule would have fed or bled another but applies too late, are called counterfeeding and counterbleeding.Holds when Raising applies to the diphthong /aɪ/ as a unit before a voiceless consonant, as in Canadian English; the g-deletion analysis is the classical /ng/ analysis of English [ŋ].

Rules rewrite strings, so the output of one rule is the input of the next. Each rule's environment is a feature pattern (2.5), and an earlier rule can create that pattern (nasal assimilation produces the [ŋ] that g-deletion needs) or erase it (flapping turns a voiceless /t/, which raising needs to see, into a voiced tap). Because the rules are not independent, the data decide the order: of the k!k!k! possible orders only those whose derivations match the attested pronunciations are admissible, and the tool counts the sites each order creates or destroys to show which relation you get.With kkk distinct rules, an ordering uses each rule once. The permutation count (comb 1.5) gives k(k−1)⋯1=k!k(k-1)\cdots1=k!k(k−1)⋯1=k! possible sequences, because the next position has one fewer unused rule. Testing those sequences against the forms then selects the admissible orders. Different orders may produce identical outputs, so the factorial counts rule sequences, not distinct surface grammars or meanings.

Choose a pair of rules and an order. The derivation table applies the first rule, then the second, to every underlying form and compares the result with the attested surface form; wrong rows turn red. The readout counts, over all forms, how many application sites the second rule has before and after the first one applies: more sites means feeding, fewer means bleeding. Flip the order and see the opposite relation (counterbleeding or counterfeeding) and which order the data want.

Think of word forms as a code for meanings. If every word cost the same, nothing would be saved; with costs growing with length, an efficient code (as in Huffman or Morse coding) gives its shortest codewords to its most probable messages. Words like the, of, I are short, and long words (unforgettable) are rare; clippings such as phone from telephone are the historical mechanism. The correlation is far from perfect: rare short words (ox, awl) and frequent long ones exist.The coding argument uses a safe exchange (algo 10.3). text.text: Uniform information density (UID) proposes that speakers tend to avoid peaks and troughs of information per unit, within grammatical and processing constraints. Levy and Jaeger study optional relative-clause that in spontaneous American English, as in “How big is the family (that) you cook for?” Their2006 study uses 3,452 eligible relative clauses from Switchboard; less predictable clause onsets are associated with more overt marking after control variables. This is evidence in one production setting, not a universal rule that adding a word improves a sentence.Holds when The source is a spoken relative-clause study, not a complement-clause or written-corpus replication. The widget is an authored ideal cue model, not fitted corpus data or a reproduction of its regressions. It treats “that” as revealing the clause without a separate production-choice surprisal, and assumes the same lexical probability with or without the cue, in the spirit of the source's pseudo-English comparison (§4, footnote 4). Other words have fixed illustrative surprisals. The quadratic objective and per-word cost are declared assumptions; real durations, ambiguity, speaker goals and correlated cues are outside this illustration.

Their Eq. 2 splits a relative-clause onset's surprisal into structural and lexical terms. text.text: A speech sound is produced by a source and shaped by a filter. The source is either the quasi-periodic puffs of air let through by the vibrating vocal folds (voicing), turbulent noise at a narrowing (whisper, aspiration, frication), or both. The filter is the air in the vocal tract from the larynx to the lips (and the nose, when the velum is lowered), whose resonances, the formants, depend on its shape; the radiated sound is the flow at the lips, differentiated by radiation into the open air. If the tract is treated as a linear, time-invariant system over stretches of a few tens of milliseconds, the output spectrum is the product P(f)=S(f) T(f) R(f),LP(f)=LS(f)+LT(f)+LR(f)(decibels),\begin{aligned}P(f)&=S(f)\,T(f)\,R(f),\\L_P(f)&=L_S(f)+L_T(f)\\&\quad+L_R(f)\quad\text{(decibels),}\end{aligned}P(f)LP​(f)​=S(f)T(f)R(f),=LS​(f)+LT​(f)+LR​(f)(decibels),​ of the source spectrum SSS (lines at the harmonics kf0k f_0kf0​ of the voice, falling about 12 dB per octave, or a flat noise continuum), the tract's transfer function TTT (peaks at the formants) and the radiation characteristic RRR (rising about 6 dB per octave). The larynx and the articulators work independently: the vocal folds set pitch and voice quality, the tongue, lips and jaw set the formants.Holds when Holds when the vocal tract can be treated as a linear, time-invariant filter (sound pressures far below the steady airflow, shapes changing slowly compared with the period) and the source is unaffected by the tract. It is only approximate when the two interact: high voices whose f0f_0f0​ approaches F1, rapid articulatory movements, and nasal coupling, which adds antiresonances.

Because the tract filters linearly, convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, so each harmonic of the source is simply scaled by the gain of the filter at its frequency. A periodic source has a line spectrum (its Fourier series), so voiced speech is a picket fence of harmonics whose heights trace the filter's resonance curve, while a noise source gives a continuous spectrum with the same peaks. The idea goes back to Johannes Müller's experiments with excised larynges in the 1830s; Chiba and Kajiyama (1941) computed the tract's resonances, and Gunnar Fant's Acoustic Theory of Speech Production (1960) made source × filter the standard model; the formant model of timbre is music-4.10.The harmonic-by-harmonic step uses the LTI eigenfunction calculation (sig 3.9): for an absolutely integrable impulse response hhh, inserting eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt in the convolution integral gives eiωt∫h(τ)e−iωτ dτe^{i\omega t}\int h(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\taueiωt∫h(τ)e−iωτdτ. Thus each harmonic retains its frequency and acquires the transfer factor at that frequency. Apply this integral calculation to the tract response when that hypothesis holds over a fixed-shape window. Neither step asserts exact linearity or independence of the source and tract in actual speech.

text.text: Model the vocal tract as a uniform tube of length LLL (about 17 cm for an adult man, 14.5 cm for a woman), closed at the glottis, where the folds are nearly shut, and open at the lips. Plane sound waves in it resonate when the tube holds an odd number of quarter wavelengths, i.e. at Fn=(2n−1) c4L,n=1,2,3,…\begin{gathered}F_n=\frac{(2n-1)\,c}{4L},\\n=1,2,3,\ldots\end{gathered}Fn​=4L(2n−1)c​,n=1,2,3,…​ With c≈350c\approx350c≈350 m/s in warm humid air and L=17.5L=17.5L=17.5 cm this gives 500, 1500, 2500 Hz: the formants of the neutral vowel schwa [ə]. Narrowing the tube changes the resonances in a predictable way: a constriction near a maximum of the volume velocity of a mode (a pressure node) lowers that formant, while one near a pressure maximum raises it. A tube open at both ends would instead resonate at n c/2Ln\,c/2Lnc/2L.Holds when Holds for plane-wave propagation, i.e. below roughly 4–5 kHz where the tube's width is small compared with the wavelength, ignoring losses (which broaden the peaks), the yielding walls and the nasal side branch. A real tract is curved and non-uniform; the uniform tube describes only the neutral vowel, and other vowels are perturbations of it.

At a closed end the air cannot move (volume velocity zero, pressure maximal); at an open end the pressure is atmospheric (pressure zero). The standing waves that fit these conditions have a quarter, three quarters, five quarters … of a wavelength in the tube, as for a stopped organ pipe (music-3.3). For non-uniform shapes the tube is cut into short sections and the transfer matrices of the sections are multiplied; resonances are the frequencies where the volume velocity at the glottis vanishes for unit flow at the lips. Perturbation theory explains the direction of the shifts: narrowing a section increases the kinetic (inertial) energy stored where the air moves fast and decreases the potential (compressional) energy where the pressure swings, so the sign of (kinetic − potential) energy density, the sensitivity function, tells whether that formant falls or rises (ling-1.7).For the stated lossless uniform tube, a harmonic pressure amplitude satisfies P′′+(ω/c)2P=0P''+(\omega/c)^2P=0P′′+(ω/c)2P=0. Converting angular frequency to hertz yields the displayed odd-quarter-wave formula. This boundary calculation is for pressure, not the opposite node convention for volume velocity.

text.text: The same vowel spoken by different people has very different formant frequencies: children's formants are up to 40–50 % higher than men's because their vocal tracts are shorter, and women's lie in between. In raw hertz the vowel categories of a population therefore overlap heavily (a child's [ʊ] can have the formants of a man's [ʌ]), yet listeners identify vowels across speakers almost effortlessly. They do so by normalising: judging each vowel relative to the speaker's own vowel space. Computational normalisations that rescale each speaker's formants, for example the log-mean method (Nearey), which subtracts the speaker's mean log formant, or Lobanov's z-scores, which standardise each formant by the speaker's mean and standard deviation, make the categories of different speakers line up and greatly reduce the overlap.

To a first approximation a shorter vocal tract multiplies all formants by the same factor (resonances scale as 1/L1/L1/L, ling-1.8), so on a logarithmic scale a speaker's whole vowel space is shifted rigidly. Subtracting the speaker's mean log formant undoes that shift (Nearey 1978); Lobanov's (1971) z-scores also undo differences in the spread of the space. Listeners appear to use similar information, both from the other vowels they have heard from the speaker (extrinsic normalisation) and from cues within the vowel such as f0f_0f0​ and F3 (intrinsic). Subtraction therefore leaves every centred log coordinate unchanged. This exact invariance belongs to the common-multiplier model; unequal formant scaling, different vowel sampling and biological differences are not removed by that identity.

When listeners hear a continuum of synthetic syllables whose voice onset time increases in equal steps from [ba] to [pa], they do not hear a gradual change: identification stays near 100 % /b/ up to a boundary (about 25 ms VOT for English labials), then switches to /p/ within one or two steps. Discrimination follows the labels: two stimuli 20 ms apart are told apart well when they straddle the boundary and barely above chance when both fall in the same category, although the acoustic difference is the same. Perception of this kind, where discrimination is predicted by identification, is called categorical perception. It is strong for stop consonants and much weaker for vowels, and it is shaped by the listener's language: the boundary sits where the language's categories need it.

If listeners could only compare category labels, the probability of answering an ABX trial correctly (is X the same as A or as B?) would be 12+12(pA−pB)2\tfrac12+\tfrac12(p_A-p_B)^221​+21​(pA​−pB​)2, where pA,pBp_A, p_BpA​,pB​ are the probabilities of labelling A and B as /p/: discrimination is then at chance within a category and peaks at the boundary. Liberman, Harris, Hoffman and Griffith (1957) found that real discrimination of stop continua nearly matches this prediction. Later work showed it is not purely categorical (listeners do hear some within-category differences, given sensitive tasks), and that chinchillas and infants show similar VOT boundaries, so part of the effect is auditory; but the boundary's location is tuned by experience with a language (ling-1.5).The label-only ABX prediction assumes fresh independent Bernoulli labels for A, B and X, with probabilities pA,pBp_A,p_BpA​,pB​ of the /p/ label, and balanced choices of whether X repeats A or B. When A and B receive the same label, the decision is a random tie; otherwise it matches X's label. Factoring products of these bounded independent label indicators (prob 2.1.13) and summing the eight label outcomes gives 12+12(pA−pB)2\tfrac12+\tfrac12(p_A-p_B)^221​+21​(pA​−pB​)2. Independence and the tie rule are premises of this prediction, not measured properties of a listener, so the formula is not a universal discrimination law.

The dispersion theory of vowel systems (Liljencrants and Lindblom, 1972) proposes that languages choose vowels that are as far apart as possible in auditory space, so that they are easy to tell apart. Model each vowel as a point in the space of possible vowels, measured by its first two formants on an auditory (Bark) scale, and choose nnn points that minimise the total "energy" E=∑i<j1/dij2E=\sum_{i<j}1/d_{ij}^2E=∑i<j​1/dij2​, where dijd_{ij}dij​ is the auditory distance between vowels iii and jjj. The optima for small nnn reproduce the patterns of the commonest inventories of the world's languages: three vowels go to the corners [i a u], and five spread into two front, one low and two back vowels, the pattern of the most frequent system [i e a o u]. For larger nnn the simple model predicts too many high vowels (central [ɨ]-like vowels) compared with real languages, which add mid vowels instead, such as the common seven-vowel [i e ɛ a ɔ o u].Holds when A model of which vowel qualities languages prefer, valid statistically across languages rather than for any one language; it ignores length, nasality, rounding as a separate dimension, and the role of focal (stable) vowels, and it overpredicts high vowels for systems of more than about seven.

The repulsive energy pushes points apart like charges confined to a region, so they first occupy the corners of the vowel space and then spread along its edge: the edge is longest along the front–back dimension at the top (high vowels have the widest F2 range), so the optimum fills the periphery and avoids the centre. The space itself is the triangle-like region reachable by the vocal tract, here the hull of the measured cardinal vowels (ling-1.9). Weighting F2 less (because higher formants are perceived less sharply) shrinks the top edge and improves the predictions for larger systems, an observation that led to refinements such as Schwartz and colleagues' dispersion–focalisation theory (1997).The ideal energy minimisation has an existence argument distinct from finding it numerically. For n≥2n\ge2n≥2 points in a compact auditory region containing nnn distinct feasible points, choose one collision-free configuration with finite energy E0E_0E0​. In its energy sublevel, every pair has distance at least E0−1/2E_0^{-1/2}E0−1/2​, so that sublevel is compact and avoids collisions. The energy is continuous there; the extreme-value theorem (pma 4.16) gives a minimum, also global since every lower-energy configuration lies in this sublevel. This proves existence in the declared model, not that a numerical search certifies the global minimum or that real languages optimise this objective.

The shaded region is the space of possible vowels (outline of the cardinal vowels, on Bark scales: F2 leftward, F1 downward). Choose the number of vowels and watch them repel each other to the configuration of least energy; each settles next to the nearest cardinal vowel symbol, named in the readout. Drag any vowel to disturb the system and see the others rearrange; Shake starts again from new random positions (the energy has local minima, so the best of ten starts is animated). Raise the F2 weight to 1 to see the model add extra high vowels, its best-known failure; lower it and mid vowels appear instead.

text.text: Phonemes are not atoms but bundles of binary distinctive features such as [±voice][\pm\text{voice}][±voice], [±nasal][\pm\text{nasal}][±nasal] and [±continuant][\pm\text{continuant}][±continuant]: each feature names one articulatory or acoustic property, and a segment is a column of +++ and −-− values (or 000, "not applicable"). A small number of features (a few dozen at most) suffices to tell apart the phonemes of any language, and phonological patterns are stated over features rather than over lists of sounds.

Each feature carves the inventory into two halves, so nnn binary features can distinguish up to 2n2^n2n segments; real inventories are far sparser than that because features are correlated (every nasal is voiced and sonorant). The reason to prefer features to symbols is that sounds sharing a feature behave alike in rules (2.4, 2.5): the set of sounds that trigger a rule is then a conjunction of feature values, a simple object, rather than an arbitrary list. The feature set used here is a simplified teaching system of 17 features: stridency, laterality and tenseness are handled coarsely, and [bk] is left unspecified (0) for schwa.The binary capacity count uses the product rule (comb 1.1): for nnn freely specifiable features with two values each, choosing one value at each coordinate gives exactly 2n2^n2n distinct bundles. An actual inventory occupies only some bundles because its features need not vary independently. The widget's value 000 means unspecified or inapplicable; it is not silently counted as one of the two signs in that binary bound.

Left: set each feature to +++, −-− or any (click a box). Right: the symbols that match every condition light up. Click a symbol on the chart to load its full feature column, then relax a feature to see which sounds join it; the presets set up classes you will meet in 2.4. Notice how few features it takes to isolate a single sound.

A set of segments is a natural class if some bundle of feature values picks out exactly its members and nothing else. Phonological rules overwhelmingly apply to, or are triggered by, natural classes, and the smaller the bundle needed, the more natural (and more frequent) the class. A set like {p,s,η,a}\{p, s, \eta, \mathrm{a}\}{p,s,η,a} that no bundle singles out is unnatural: any bundle covering all of its members also covers extra segments.

The segments matching a feature value form a set; a bundle selects the intersection of such sets. So natural classes are exactly the intersections of feature-value sets (2.3), a tiny family compared with all 2392^{39}239 subsets of the 39 symbols on the chart. To test a given set, intersect the feature values it shares: that intersection is the most specific bundle containing the whole set, and the set is natural exactly when this bundle selects nothing else. The tool then searches for the shortest bundle with the same extension.Make one predicate for each specified feature value, true of a segment exactly when that segment carries that value. Conjunction has the truth-table semantics of logic 2.3, so a bundle holds exactly when every selected predicate holds; its extension is therefore the intersection of their extensions. A 000 entry is not automatically the negation of a positive feature value. This is a finite interpretation on the displayed inventory, and it licenses the intersection test without treating arbitrary subsets as single natural classes.

Click symbols to build a set (gold). The readout finds the smallest feature bundle that defines it, or shows the smallest natural class that contains it — the extra members it drags in are marked red. Try the preset plural -s triggers (p t k f θ): it is natural, defined by the three values [+cons −voi −strid], which is why one rule suffices in 2.5. Then add /s/ or /ɑ/ and watch it stop being natural.

When a grammar has several rules, the order in which they apply can change the output. Rule XXX feeds rule YYY when applying XXX first creates new sites where YYY can apply, and bleeds it when applying XXX first destroys sites where YYY would apply. If the attested forms need XXX before YYY in the first case or YYY before XXX in the second, the order is extrinsic and must be part of the grammar. The reverse orders, in which a rule would have fed or bled another but applies too late, are called counterfeeding and counterbleeding.Holds when Raising applies to the diphthong /aɪ/ as a unit before a voiceless consonant, as in Canadian English; the g-deletion analysis is the classical /ng/ analysis of English [ŋ].

Rules rewrite strings, so the output of one rule is the input of the next. Each rule's environment is a feature pattern (2.5), and an earlier rule can create that pattern (nasal assimilation produces the [ŋ] that g-deletion needs) or erase it (flapping turns a voiceless /t/, which raising needs to see, into a voiced tap). Because the rules are not independent, the data decide the order: of the k!k!k! possible orders only those whose derivations match the attested pronunciations are admissible, and the tool counts the sites each order creates or destroys to show which relation you get.With kkk distinct rules, an ordering uses each rule once. The permutation count (comb 1.5) gives k(k−1)⋯1=k!k(k-1)\cdots1=k!k(k−1)⋯1=k! possible sequences, because the next position has one fewer unused rule. Testing those sequences against the forms then selects the admissible orders. Different orders may produce identical outputs, so the factorial counts rule sequences, not distinct surface grammars or meanings.

Choose a pair of rules and an order. The derivation table applies the first rule, then the second, to every underlying form and compares the result with the attested surface form; wrong rows turn red. The readout counts, over all forms, how many application sites the second rule has before and after the first one applies: more sites means feeding, fewer means bleeding. Flip the order and see the opposite relation (counterbleeding or counterfeeding) and which order the data want.

Levy and Jaeger study optional relative-clause that in spontaneous American English, as in “How big is the family (that) you cook for?” Their2006 study uses 3,452 eligible relative clauses from Switchboard; less predictable clause onsets are associated with more overt marking after control variables.
